name: Sines
title: Ship UTM Sines: Thickness Gauging at Berth and Anchor
description: Thickness measurement at Sines for container ships, crude tankers and LNG carriers: UTM at Terminal XXI and the energy berths, CAP and pre-docking gauging.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships at the Port of Sines
intro: Sines is Portugal's deep-water Atlantic port: a container transhipment hub at Terminal XXI and an energy port serving the Galp refinery, the petrochemical complex and the REN LNG terminal. The ships are large container ships, crude and product tankers and LNG carriers, and their calls are short. Superintendents call us to gauge ballast tanks, deck and hull structure at berth or anchor, usually ahead of a docking at Setúbal or elsewhere. We mobilise a team from India to Sines, planned around the anchorage wait or the call.
keywords: container ship gauging at terminal xxi

highlights.p: Container ships at Terminal XXI and tankers at the energy berths call briefly. Gauging concentrates on the flagged ballast tanks, deck structure and scrubber piping that matter most for the next docking.
A laden crude tanker or LNG carrier waiting off Sines has empty ballast tanks, which makes the anchorage the right place for ballast-tank and inner-hull gauging before berthing.
Sines is not a ship-repair port. Readings taken here go into the repair specification for a docking at Lisnave's Setúbal yard or elsewhere, so steel renewal is agreed early.

port.h: The port of Sines and its traffic
p: Sines lies on the open Atlantic coast of the Alentejo, south of Lisbon. Unlike Lisbon it is not an estuary port: breakwaters protect deep-water berths built on an exposed coast, which is what lets it take very large container ships and crude tankers. The port is organised around specialised terminals rather than a city waterfront, with Terminal XXI for containers, the liquid bulk terminal for crude and refined products, a petrochemical terminal, the LNG terminal and a multipurpose terminal, all backed by the industrial zone behind the port.

Terminal XXI, operated by PSA Sines and under expansion, handles container ships on deep-sea mainline and transhipment services, with feeder ships distributing containers onwards to other Iberian and Atlantic ports. On the energy side, the liquid bulk terminal serves Galp's Sines refinery, bringing in crude tankers and loading product tankers; the petrochemical terminal adds chemical tankers; and the REN LNG terminal receives LNG carriers supplying Portugal's gas network. Bulk carriers and general cargo ships use the multipurpose terminal, so the port sees most deep-sea ship types, from feeders to very large container ships, within a compact set of berths.

Calls at Sines are fast: container ships work to tight transhipment windows, and tankers berth, discharge or load, and sail. The gauging opportunities therefore come from waiting time at the anchorage off the port, where ships wait for a berth, a cargo or orders, and from the occasional planned lay-by. Because Sines is not a ship-repair port, gauging here is almost always preparation for a docking elsewhere, most often at the Lisnave yard at Setúbal up the coast or at yards in Spain and further afield. The readings therefore feed the repair specification rather than a survey in progress, and their value lies in arriving at the yard with the steel renewal already estimated.

facilities.h: Gauging at the Sines terminals and anchorage
p: Container ship gauging at Terminal XXI is fitted into the call. The team boards once the ship is secured, works in double-bottom, side and wing ballast tanks and on deck structure clear of the crane lanes, and leaves holds that are being worked. On the largest ships a single call is rarely enough for a full renewal-survey scope, so the useful product is targeted: known problem areas, the ballast tanks the class has flagged for substantial corrosion, and scrubber wash-water and overboard piping, which many large container ships now carry.

Tanker gauging at Sines follows the liquid bulk terminal's safety rules: cargo tanks are not entered during cargo operations, and electronic instruments on deck in hazardous zones need permission. The practical approach is ballast-tank gauging at the anchorage before berthing, when a laden crude tanker or LNG carrier has empty ballast tanks. The anchorage is on an open coast, so Atlantic swell and wind decide whether launch transfers can run, and the plan carries a weather allowance from the start. Product tankers loading at the refinery berths reverse the timing: they arrive with ballast tanks full and empty them during loading, so gauging fits the departure side if the schedule allows.
list: Terminal XXI (PSA Sines) — targeted ballast-tank, deck and scrubber piping gauging on large container ships within the transhipment window.
Liquid bulk terminal — ballast-tank and deck gauging on crude and product tankers serving the Galp refinery, within the terminal's permit rules.
REN LNG terminal — ballast-tank and inner-hull readings from the ballast side on LNG carriers, coordinated with gas-safety requirements.
Petrochemical terminal — ballast-tank and deck gauging on chemical tankers, with cargo tanks left for a gas-free docking.
Sines anchorage — launch-served pre-docking gauging on laden tankers and waiting container ships, subject to Atlantic swell.
Multipurpose terminal — hold, hatch coaming and ballast-tank gauging on bulk carriers and general cargo ships during their stay.

context.h: Regulation and market context at Sines
p: Portugal applies port state control under the Paris MoU, and the deep-sea ships calling at Sines, some of the largest afloat, are subject to the same risk-based targeting as at any EU port. The EU ETS (since 2024) and FuelEU Maritime (since 2025) apply to every call, and the ETS has made the location of transhipment hubs a commercial question for container lines; Sines is an EU hub on the Atlantic side of the Strait of Gibraltar. For gauging purposes the point is simpler: the container ships and tankers here are large, often older, and on tight rotations, so time at anchor is the only time most of them offer.

No sulphur ECA applies off the Alentejo coast yet. September 2028 ends that, when the 0.10% sulphur limit of the North-East Atlantic ECA, adopted at MEPC 84 and in force from 1 September 2027, starts to apply in mainland Portuguese waters; from then the container ships and tankers calling here will either burn ECA-compliant fuel or run their scrubbers in ECA mode on the approach. Tankers loading and discharging here are ESP ships, gauged under IACS UR Z10.4 if they are double-hull oil tankers or Z10.3 if they are chemical tankers, and vetting departments and charterers commonly look for CAP once a tanker passes about 15 years. Container ships and LNG carriers sit outside the ESP regime, so UR Z7 and the society's own rules set the extent of their gauging.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Sines
jobs.p: Sines jobs are short and opportunistic, built around an anchorage wait or a call window, and they almost always prepare a docking elsewhere. We ask for the ETA, the terminal line-up, the class's outstanding requirements and the draft yard specification, then size the team to the time available and the weather outlook. Tanker gauging at Sines and container work typically look like this:
list: Pre-docking gauging of double-bottom and wing ballast tanks on a laden crude tanker at the Sines anchorage, ahead of its CAP docking at Setúbal.
Targeted gauging of hatch coamings, deck longitudinals and two flagged ballast tanks on a large container ship during a Terminal XXI transhipment call.
Wall-thickness checks at fixed points on a container ship's scrubber wash-water and overboard lines during a Terminal XXI call, giving the owner a trend before Atlantic ECA running starts.
LNG carrier thickness gauging at anchor before berthing at the REN terminal: ballast tanks and the inner hull from the ballast side, for the ship's intermediate survey plan.
On-hire condition gauging of holds and ballast tanks on a bulk carrier at the multipurpose terminal, documenting steel condition for the charterer.

logistics: The team flies into Lisbon Humberto Delgado Airport and continues south to Sines by road; Faro Airport in the Algarve is an alternative for some routings. The ship's agent arranges ISPS passes and terminal inductions at Terminal XXI, the liquid bulk terminal or the LNG terminal, and launch boats for ships at the anchorage. Each technician travels on a Schengen visa issued in India; we apply once the call or docking is firm and ask for an invitation letter from the owner or agent. Because an open-coast anchorage is weather-dependent, boarding times are confirmed with the agent close to the day.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a container ship during a transhipment call at Terminal XXI?
faqs.a: Yes, within the call window. We concentrate on what the superintendent most needs, such as flagged ballast tanks, hatch coamings, deck longitudinals and scrubber piping, and work clear of the cranes. A full renewal-survey scope on a large container ship needs more time than a transhipment call gives, so that is planned for the docking, with the Sines readings used to firm up the steel estimate.

faqs.q: Where do ships calling at Sines go for drydocking?
faqs.a: Sines is not a ship-repair port. The nearest large repair yard is Lisnave's Mitrena yard at Setúbal, up the coast, and ships also dock in Spain and further afield. Hull inspection at Sines is therefore preparation: the readings go into the repair specification so the yard and the owner agree the steel renewal before the ship arrives.

faqs.q: Is the Sines anchorage workable for launch-boat transfers?
faqs.a: Usually, but it is an open Atlantic coast. Swell and wind decide whether launches run and whether the pilot ladder is safe, so we include a weather allowance in the plan, keep tank work for once the team is on board, and settle with the agent beforehand how the team will leave the ship if conditions worsen during the job.

faqs.q: Can you gauge an LNG carrier before it berths at the Sines LNG terminal?
faqs.a: Yes, at anchor and with the master's agreement. On a laden arrival the ballast tanks are empty, so the double bottom, side ballast tanks and the inner hull, measured from the ballast side, can be gauged before berthing. Work at the terminal itself is limited by its gas-safety rules, so anything not reached at anchor is planned into the ship's next docking.
